text: The centrepiece of this ecosystem is Infinite Studios, which houses Singapore's largest sound stages.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The sound stages face stiff competition from the likes of Pinewood Studios in Iskandar, Johor.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: As such, the sound stages in Singapore have not seen the expected scale of projects.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And to make viable use of the space, these state-of-the-art stages are now being leased out for alternative uses like Fashion Shows and Corporate events.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: One big issue is the lack of skilled Singaporean manpower to operate these sound stages.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Most Singapore film students and practitioners prefer to go down the art film route, the route which has unearthed world-class talent, such as Anthony Chen, Boo Junfeng, K Rajagopal and Kirsten Tan, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And while we must encourage our filmmakers to pursue their dreams, there are also massive job opportunities in mass market, commercial projects.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We need to help educate and incentivise Singaporeans to fill these jobs.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: More and more film studios and television platforms are looking to produce their mega projects in this region.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, pan regional pay television networks and digital platforms are specifically looking to produce original content in this region, as this is becoming a requirement for the renewal of their carriage licences in many markets.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, given the infrastructure available, there is a real opportunity for our talents to scale up to international industry standards and become familiar with production facilities like sound stages.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, IMDA can look into this and see how we can help with incentives and training schemes to fill this gap.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore can then be an attractive option for broadcasters and platforms, as we will not just have the hardware, but the software, too.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, I spoke about programmes like the daily drama series "Tanglin" on Channel 5, which seems to have struck a chord with Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Another highlight for me was the documentary "Regardless of Race".

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Produced by CNA, the one-hour documentary aired in August last year.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It made a very tough topic, perceptions of race in multicultural Singapore, accessible and entertaining.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I congratulate the commissioning editors of the programme as it was curated beautifully.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, one of the key standouts of the programme was the presenter, Minister of State Dr Janil Puthucheary.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Minister of State Janil was not just credible, but a natural in front of the camera.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Other Channel 5 programmes like "Renovaid" and "You Deserve a Break" are great examples of how impactful PSB programmes can be.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: However, while we have had a few successes, there is still a lack of consistency in the quality of programming, particularly on Channel 5.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Dramas like "P.I." still suffer from loose plots, bad acting and inferior production quality.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And while programmes like "OK Chope!" can be lauded for their innovativeness and daring, once you start watching, it is hard to continue.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The commissioning process needs to be strengthened, particularly with increased funding for online content through the new content development fund that is being set up.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The on-demand digital world is even more picky than the linear world.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Commissioners have to know exactly what their audiences are after.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This list should include details, such as genres, durations and production budgets.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Mediacorp, just like every other free to air broadcaster in the world, is facing huge challenges to retain its audience share.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Competition from the plethora of digital platforms as well as falling advertising revenues have made the broadcast landscape extremely challenging.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: One area that I had briefly alluded to earlier in my speech was in working with pan regional broadcasters and platforms, like Fox, AXN, Discovery, A&E, Netflix, Amazon and many more.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Most, if not all of these platforms, are looking to produce local and regional content.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: However, unlike free-to-air (FTA) broadcasters, they do not have production resources and often rely on independent production companies.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Mediacorp has state-of-the-art facilities in its new premises at one-north, from studios to auditoriums and broadcast facilities.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: To me, it makes sense for Mediacorp to partner these pan regional networks to produce content that can be aired on both platforms.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This will allow for bigger budgets and talent pool, thereby creating more quality content and more jobs.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It also offers a bigger platform for our local talent to be exposed as a pan regional channel typically has a footprint of 20 to 40 countries.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It can also be a source of revenue as Mediacorp can tap on years of production experience and technical knowledge to support these productions.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Given the size of the Singapore market, it would be difficult to sustain growth without forging these relationships.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Customer service has not always been at the top of the agenda for our pay channels but, in today's world of cord cutters and content on demand, it should be.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: How many times have we been put on hold for hours when we desperately needed to speak to someone because of a technical issue?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Or how many of us have suddenly realised that a channel that we were watching was suddenly taken off air or replaced by channels that are not really apple-for-apple replacements, or even programme guides that constantly give you the wrong information, and even the wrong synopses?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But for me personally, the biggest pet peeve is the football coverage.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: However, there is little evidence that the pay platform has exercised quality control over the licensee's programming, as the locally produced programming that surround the football matches is some of the worst we have seen in years.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Shoddy production values and amateur presenters have tainted and continue to taint the enjoyment of watching these matches.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is frustrating as the pay platform actually has access to the world-class and professionally produced original pre-match and half-time shows.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They need to take their customers seriously and that is the only way to stay relevant in an era of technological disruption.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: However, the Government can only do so much.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, it is up to the industry and society at large to take advantage of the support and foster growth and success.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Vikram Nair, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It was the successor of our old Singapore Broadcasting Corporation (SBC).

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over the years, Mediacorp has been innovating to keep up with the times, reaching across multiple platforms in creative ways.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: With my various duties − I am sure many Members of this House have as well − I do not get the chance to watch television (TV) on a regular basis, but I do get to watch a lot of locally-produced content happily on Toggle.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, I do not have to catch a show at the exact same time, I do not have to be available at the same time, but I can still keep up with all the content that I am interested in.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And many of these locally-produced shows on Toggle are supported by PSB funding.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this allows our "Uniquely Singapore" content to have a platform and to be enjoyed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I will make a short pitch since everyone else here is doing this as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of my favourite contents on Toggle is the telemovies, but the vernacular telemovies do not come with subtitles.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As much as I would love to watch them all, I do not get a chance to.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That is my little pitch for quality improvement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Having said that, Toggle is a wonderful platform because it allows us to access content not only on TV, but also on mobile devices, so that we can watch it anywhere, whenever it is available.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, all of this requires financing, and the revolving media landscape of FTA TV is largely supported by advertising revenues, for which there is intense competition across a variety of platforms.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Government rolls out a great many good policies every year, and yet, public awareness of these may be limited.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I noticed a lot of creative approaches to bridge this gap in recent times, including helpful aids, such as kopi kaki books and videos in different languages.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a long-standing member of the Feedback Unit's Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH) panel, I am also personally aware of how hard the Government tries to reach out and have dialogues with as many groups of Singaporeans as possible in a wide variety of forums, from face-to-face dialogues, outreach posts, Facebook livechats and radio shows.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In a more diversified society and changing media landscape, it is important that the Government further strengthen public communications to ensure that we can reach out effectively to different groups of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There seems to be an occasional disconnect between the Government's genuine confidence that a full public consultation has been carried out and the ground's equally genuine consternation that they were not consulted.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I asked people for views about whether they would turn out for a Government-organised engagement to share views or issues they said they cared for and, if not, why.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I would only focus on the answers of those who currently feel less inspired to show up because I believe their specific feedback will help us design engagements that reach beyond the usual choir.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: These are just two ad verbatim answers: "Yes, if there is real interest in engagement and opposing views"; "Yes, but only if it feels like there is a genuine interest in what we have to say, not just defending certain policies or positions that have already been decided on.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It will be nice to have a session where whoever is conducting the session just ask questions and listens." Mdm Chairman, these are subjective points of view, of course.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But I do want to revisit a point I brought up in the Budget Debate on the role of facts and feelings when it comes to effective communication between the Government and the people.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I said that we are missing a big point if we say people must deal with the facts as they are, not where they feel they should be.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But most people make their choices according to their feelings about the facts.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, if we care about making sure people hear us out on the hard facts about our country's situation, we must start all our communications with connecting with people where they are, which is how they feel, even if the feeling is disagreeable or irrational to us.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If not, we have to accept that our words will never impact anyone outside our echo chambers.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Online strategies are really good for downloading facts and messages but only offline face-to-face engagement alone can do the most significant work of communication, which is communicating and building trust, not just between different groups of people but between the people and the Government.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I think there is a place for consultation sessions to be used by the Government to share with people the difficult trade-offs involved in policymaking.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But if a session becomes more about a download, then the consultation is no longer perceived as a consultation but a presentation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Once people feel they are being presented to rather than consulted, they will either choose not to show up anymore or, if they show up, they will stay silent or offer only surface answers that they may think you want to hear, rather than the deep views they really hold, which is precisely the kind of high-quality deep data that you need to formulate decisions that connect with the ground.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Many in the industry shared the Government's ambition to help young Singaporeans become more resilient and an earlier consultation could have allowed them to not just share their concerns but offer their combined years of expertise and pave the way for maybe a more win-win partnership.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Though the industry still maintains good trusting relations with the public sector partners, many still wish that the process was done a little bit differently.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Both the people and the Government want each other to not just understand but empathise with the complexity of the issues they are dealing with and the trade-offs in decision-making.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I have two suggestions to make community engagements better.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Give people a real chance to have their views shape policymaking.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: If their views have been taken into account, inform them or, better yet, celebrate them, because such trust-building goes a very long way.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Prof Tommy Koh said that including challengers who are subversive and who have alternative points of view make Singapore stronger.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Member of Parliament Louis Ng suggested that public servants work more closely with civil society activists and not to be afraid of them, because these are people who speak up because they care.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The people we engage less with may be precisely the people we need to engage more with.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My hope is for both the people and the Government to approach the consultation process as an exercise in compassion, a space to listen and share each other's passions, pains and interests.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We often forget that compassion is not a fluffy word − passion means suffering, compassion means suffering together.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Trying to do good work for our country involves plenty of suffering enough.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I hope we do work towards finding new ways of solving our sufferings together rather than apart.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Darryl David, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Indeed, we saw a segment of "Hwan Hee Chio Hor" in the video shown by the Minister earlier.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Also are there plans to use similar programmes and strategies to target the same elderly demographic in other ethnic groups, such as the Malay and Tamil communities?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Such programmes would also be able to raise issues that would be unique to those respective communities as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Aside from pay-TV, other media channels, such as Netflix and online streaming websites like YouTube, have given local audiences many options to consume media content.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: What is the Ministry doing to ensure that PSB remains relevant and accessible in this modern age where media content exist across multiple formats and platforms, and consumers are no longer tied to one single medium?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Would the Ministry explore and develop collaborations with non-mainstream providers of media content to support the dissemination of PSB?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: And needless to say, my eight-year-old son and I have used this to justify to my wife why it is okay for him to read his football magazines as opposed to his textbooks.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: My point is, Madam, I would like to enquire what the National Library Board (NLB) is doing to promote and encourage reading among young children.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Also, could NLB share what it is doing to promote a reading culture among the other demographics and ethnic groups as well?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: First, provide an update on the progress of the National Reading Movement.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Second, what measures are taken to inspire Singaporeans to read?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Common barriers to reading books include a lack of time, interest and motivation, or a combination of all three factors.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Third, set up thematic book reading clubs at community clubs, such as Travel and Leisure, Health and Medicine, Investment and Wealth, Personal Skills and Improvement.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Sun Xueling, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is obviously a place that people want to go to.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: In traditional library spaces, visitors read or do research quietly while in new types of library spaces, visitors want to have the opportunity to explore, experience and collaborate with others while learning.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: A library can be a fertile ground to inspire and inculcate the habits of lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Preschoolers, young teens, young adults and mature adults have different approaches to learning and different interests.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: It is not quite sufficient just to segregate books by reading complexity and interest.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: The layout, interactivity that visitors can enjoy, should be catered to different age groups.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: For instance, students can be engaged to serve as active volunteers in the library.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: They can interact with seniors and bridge the digitalisation gap for seniors by showing them how to use the online tools available in the library.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Seniors can then have personalised help in learning how to access learning online as well as e-Government services to make their lives more convenient.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Seniors and adults can also be encouraged to come together to organise reading programmes for preschoolers.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Not all young children have the opportunity to grow up in an environment where books are readily available or have adults to read to them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: If volunteers are able to read to them and encourage these preschoolers to take part in storytelling and role play, this would greatly enhance their confidence and readiness for school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Mr Ganesh Rajaram on the importance of partnerships in industry development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our strategy to attract global media companies has provided opportunities for local media companies and Singaporeans to participate in flagship projects and international co-productions, which can then be enjoyed by consumers in Singapore and also around the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our local production houses have also been working with international broadcasters, such as Discovery, National Geographic and Home Box Office (HBO) Asia, to produce original content for broadcast across Asia.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When I visited HBO Asia and they showed me and told me about this collaboration, I was very encouraged because it has provided opportunities for Singaporeans and our companies to be able to work hand in hand with an international company to produce something that can be enjoyed in Singapore and also exported to other markets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is an incubation programme by Mediacorp that supports media startups through seed funding, mentoring, networking and marketing opportunities through Mediacorp's platforms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Several of these startups are already partnering business units in Mediacorp to develop interesting concepts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: What IMDA does is to support this initiative and also bring in what we call the Accreditation Scheme to complement Mediapreneur's efforts to provide tailored assistance to these startups in areas, such as product testing and financial modelling.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I met some of the startups and their founders when I visited Mediapreneur.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They feel strongly about their ideas and they appreciate the support from IMDA and Mediacorp.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I look forward to seeing some of their ideas being adopted by our media companies, whether it is Mediacorp or other media companies, to produce entertaining content and to raise the level of enjoyment for our viewers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Leon Perera asked if IMDA is exploring ways to promote private sector funding of local films.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: IMDA has been studying different ideas, including the ones mentioned by Mr Perera, and has been discussing with industry players to see which ideas are more feasible and more impactful to help them to grow their business and also to produce quality content.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And because 100% of the equity goes to the media company, it is fully incentivised to commercialise the film, including taking it overseas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to study ways to boost the market for film investments, including tapping on new funding models and growing the demand for quality local content.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: IMDA's support for the local film community through grants, scholarships, these efforts have produced some encouraging results.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, IMDA has embarked on a partnership with a local online film platform, Vidsee, to create a Singapore film channel.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Today, the channel showcases a collection of short films produced by promising local filmmakers like Kirsten Tan and K Rajagopal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These are some examples of the industry development initiatives by IMDA to help our local filmmakers create compelling Singapore stories and bring their films overseas to an even wider audience.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: IMDA's Talent Assistance scheme has groomed media professionals and helped deepen their capabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: He is a freelance animator who attended two overseas training courses with funding support from IMDA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The training has enabled Billy to enhance his proficiency in storytelling and animation and helped him to secure more projects.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our growing media industry will create many jobs that require a diverse range of skills, including the use of media tools, to achieve business outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how we plan to develop a future-ready media workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, our media workforce must deepen core skills to remain competitive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We need to strengthen content creation and the ability to tell original, compelling stories.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One initiative is IMDA's Story Lab, which brings people together to incubate ideas and explore innovative ways to tell interesting stories.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also want to equip media professionals with skills to benefit from the latest technologies and platforms, including the facilities at Pixel Studios, which has been purpose-built for online content creators.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: IMDA and SkillsFuture Singapore will jointly develop this framework as a common reference for jobseekers, media professionals and employers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will contain information on current and emerging skills for different occupational levels, as well as career progression pathways for different media-related jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Employers can use this framework to design talent development plans to attract and retain talent for their companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Hence, our third focus is to provide better support for media freelancers, in line with the Ministry of Manpower's (MOM's) broader efforts to encourage fair and progressive workplaces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is done in consultation with media companies and freelancers and it will provide a list of good employment practices, such as having written contracts that clearly spell out payment terms, intellectual property rights and how to handle disputes, if they should arise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These moves aim to encourage better work relationships between media companies and freelancers, and I share Mr Ganesh Rajaram's hope that freelancers will proactively leverage on these available initiatives to help them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I also urge freelancers to focus on their career development and retirement adequacy, including contributing regularly to their CPF and MediSave accounts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These are important for their longer-term retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The fourth thrust is to partner key industry players and industry associations to develop our media professionals and propagate good practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will monitor the effectiveness of these measures and will consider introducing new measures, if necessary, to ensure that media sector employees and freelancers are fairly treated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Mr Zaqy Mohamad and Mr Darryl David that PSB is important for our national development, and it needs to stay relevant in the digital age.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through PSB, we have supported media companies to produce local programmes that entertain and engage Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dramas, such as "Tanglin", which Mr Ganesh Rajaram mentioned.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On Channel 8, we have this very popular Mandarin programme called "Yao yaoba", which means "118".

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These are very popular programmes that continue to drive primetime viewership on our FTA channels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Other genres, such as documentaries, current affairs programmes, have also been well-received.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One example is the excellent documentary on nursing produced by Channel 8's Tuesday Report.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I attended the preview and met the nurses and their families, and the viewers who have watched the episodes found them to be very meaningful and admirable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As several Members have highlighted, the media landscape is becoming increasingly challenging.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Changes are happening very quickly and we cannot stand still.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Apart from Netflix, Amazon Prime and Viu, recently I read that YouTube will be launching a new streaming television service called YouTube TV.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The selection of over-the-top content is growing rapidly, but consumers' time and attention are limited.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Even premium content on Pay TV channels no longer holds the same draw.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This has caused TV advertising revenues to decline but at a time when more investments are actually needed to build capabilities in content production and online technology.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Vikram Nair and Mr Zaqy Mohamad asked about Mediacorp's plans to better position itself for the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At last year's COS, I spoke about transforming PSB by focusing on 3Cs − Content, Channels and Capabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These remain our focus in bringing quality local programmes to all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I recently read a Straits Times interview of Mediacorp's award-winning scriptwriter, Mr Ang Eng Tee.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: He is a script writer for many of the popular Channel 8 dramas − "Hero", "Yao Yao Ba" that I have mentioned earlier, and previously "The Little Nonya".

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And what Mr Ang shared when he was interviewed by the Straits Times was that the challenge to get eyeballs for local TV will increase, but he said, "If we continue to tell Singaporean stories, there will be something here for Singaporeans to watch".

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Locally-produced PSB programmes can best capture and convey our unique Singaporean flavour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But we cannot match the budgets of Hollywood productions or Korean dramas, so we must compete differently by engaging our viewers through quality local content.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We all know digital is the new frontier, especially so for younger viewers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mediacorp has been moving towards a stronger digital focus over the past few years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will invest in further improving Toggle as its online platform so that we can watch our favourite local programmes anytime, anywhere and on any device, from mobile phones to large-screen high-definition TVs (HDTVs).

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Toggle has seen a three-fold increase in unique viewers since its relaunch in April 2015.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I must say this is an encouraging improvement, considering the intense competition for eyeballs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This growth is helped by the first slate of Toggle Original series which was well-received.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, it goes back to what we discussed earlier, that content is, ultimately, the most important thing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Good-quality local content is what I think will help to drive viewership.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will support Mediacorp to boost its Toggle offerings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This year, Mediacorp will roll out an even bigger slate of Toggle Originals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These will involve collaboration with independent producers and tertiary institutions and cover a diverse spectrum of genres to offer more content choices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For better user experience, Toggle will also enhance its streaming reliability, navigation, content recommendation and personalisation features.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I was glad to hear Mr Vikram Nair spoke earlier about watching his favourite shows on Toggle, and we will certainly look into his suggestion for Mediacorp to add subtitles so that the shows can be enjoyed by more people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Even as Mediacorp strengthens its digital channels, FTA TV channels remain important for many viewers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: FTA channels are collectively still the most popular destination for Singaporeans when it comes to media consumption.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Last month, our first local bilingual TV series for preschoolers "Junction Tree" was shown on Okto.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This series is supported by IMDA and the Lee Kuan Yew Fund for Bilingualism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mediacorp has also started featuring sports programmes, including programmes that encourage young Singaporeans to take an interest in sports and lead active lifestyles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One example is Okto Cup, a futsal tournament for kids.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I want to thank her and acknowledge her suggestion and we have discussed with Mediacorp how best we can focus on this area.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Because I agree with her, it is very important to provide good-quality programmes for our children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes enhancing training in core skills, such as commissioning, directing, storytelling and content production.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through new scholarship and apprenticeship programmes, as well as collaborations with schools, we want to discover our young talent and then groom them early in media and content production.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes a programme to develop young producers to create content targeted at youths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, content produced by young people for young people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Darryl David asked how the local media industry has benefited from increased Government support for PSB.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through PSB, Mediacorp outsources a portion of its programmes to independent production houses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will also explore more co-production opportunities, a point mentioned by Mr Ganesh Rajaram.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I will certainly discuss with Mediacorp to see how we can do this better − it is a win-win partnership − so that it benefits Mediacorp and it benefits our film industry, our media industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The scheme is now in its fifth year, and our partnership with platforms like Starhub has produced good programmes, such as "Echoes of Time", a historical drama series by Ochre Pictures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It received a nomination for Best Production Design and Art Direction at the 2016 New York Festivals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Another initiative is Singapore Press Holdings' (SPHs') partnership with IMDA to produce and distribute short-form digital video content.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The aim is to connect younger Singaporeans with digital PSB content and encourage a greater appreciation for our local productions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I viewed the recent video produced by Zaobao on the world's languages and must say they did a good job. 继 续 加 油！ I agree with Mr Zaqy Mohamad that high-quality journalism is an important public good which we must continue to support and preserve in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Like Mediacorp, SPH is keenly aware of the need to engage the digital generation, and they are actively reinventing themselves to better serve their readers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I met the online teams from The Straits Times and Lianhe Zaobao.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They are doing good work in producing interesting digital content, trying out new ideas and fresh approaches.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have to continue to work at it, but it is good sign, it is an encouraging sign that people find newspapers' content in Singapore to be satisfactory and their ranking has improved.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This result is commendable, especially in a challenging period when many overseas newspapers are seeing declining readership.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Measuring and analysing data give a better feel of the concerns and sentiments of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This helps us to address information gaps, respond more quickly and customise more impactful messages.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MCI will enhance our data analytics and research capabilities, which will help to support whole-of-Government communications efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I agree with Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin that the Government must engage widely and meaningfully.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Progress has been made over the years, including use of face-to-face sessions, to engage in deep conversations and candid discussions with different groups of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MCI is a strong supporter of public engagement, an important area driven by the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, REACH has worked with other Government agencies and partners to increase its number of outreach sessions which include dialogues, focus group discussions and also listening points.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We welcome suggestions on how we can further improve.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Effective listening and engagement are an important part of effective communications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are also collaborating with partners to produce innovative content that can connect with Singaporeans, both intellectually and emotionally.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The winners come from different backgrounds but they share a common passion for filmmaking.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through this co-creation initiative, we hope to encourage greater involvement from the community and bring fresh perspectives on complex social issues.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The four teams are currently developing their story ideas into short films, which will be ready next month.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Darryl David asked if we plan to continue with our public communications efforts in vernacular languages, including the use of dialect, to communicate with seniors and help them understand Government policies and programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MCI has produced dialect programmes together with Mediacorp and industry partners like Jack Neo and Royston Tan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These programmes communicate useful information to seniors through an entertaining format and using a language which they are familiar with.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To reinforce the messages, we also engage our seniors through roadshows in our HDB heartlands and through key touchpoints like the Pioneer Generation Ambassador network.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over the years, MCI has worked with Mediacorp to enhance the coverage of Parliamentary proceedings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Today, key Parliament sessions, such as the Budget Statement and the Opening of Parliament, are broadcast "live" on both TV and online.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Footage of all Parliament speeches and Question and Answer sessions are already available online on CNA's Parliament microsite.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Parliamentary highlights are loaded onto this microsite within three hours of broadcast.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Videos of all speeches and footage from Question Time are uploaded by the following morning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If you go to the site, you will see that the videos are sorted by date and name of the Member of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The video clips are easily accessible by the public and are organised for convenient viewing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition, the public has access to the full written record of Parliamentary proceedings via the online Hansard.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singaporeans who are interested in watching the proceedings can also attend any Parliamentary Sitting in person, watch the news on TV that evening, or view the complete set of video clips from the CNA microsite using their computers and mobile devices the next morning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Based on data collected, the viewership of "live" broadcasts remains low.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The experiences in other countries show that there are pros and cons to having "live" broadcasts of parliament proceedings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Observers have noted that one downside is the risk of members of parliament playing to the gallery in the presence of live cameras, which would affect the work of parliament.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I believe these existing avenues have been useful in helping Singaporeans to understand what was discussed in this House and to inform their decisions on national policies and legislative changes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Several Members have asked about our plans to promote a reading culture in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Please allow me to conclude my speech in Mandarin to talk about our efforts to promote reading in Chinese.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Government launched the National Reading Movement last year to encourage Singaporeans to read regularly, read widely and read together with the family.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: A key focus is to promote reading in mother tongue languages with the aim to strengthen the standard of bilingualism in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Stanley Chia, the founder of an educational startup Cialfo, is a businessman who benefited from being bilingual.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: He told me that his Mandarin was not fluent in the past but, with more exposure and frequent use, his standard of Chinese has improved.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is especially helpful for his business in China.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the beginning, Stanley had a more limited vocabulary in Chinese.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: However, with persistent hard work and practice, he can now use fluent Mandarin to make speeches and conduct meetings, thereby building very good relationships with his clients.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: NLB has rolled out Tiny Tots Reading Club to encourage young children to read in Chinese through many interesting activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are currently five such reading clubs for children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: NLB will expand this to more libraries around Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I had the opportunity to participate in some of these reading sessions when I visited the library and was glad to see many parents showing keen interest in encouraging their children to read Chinese books, including books written by our local authors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Besides children, NLB will also be expanding its collaboration with our media partners to encourage more adults to read in Chinese.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These sessions will cover a range of interesting topics from finance and health to local Chinese literature.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Here, I would like to thank our media partners for supporting these initiatives, helping us to encourage more people to read widely.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Reading together in the community can cultivate a deeper appreciation of our culture and heritage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This requires support from our community partners and the general public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We would like to thank our volunteers for running the library at Chinatown.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chou was the founder of Popular Holdings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As a passionate lover of Chinese culture, he had been a strong supporter.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On behalf of NLB, I would like to express our sincere appreciation to the late Mr Chou and his family for their generous donation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: They also herald change − uncomfortable in many ways, but necessary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This is why learning to adapt, to keep on picking up new knowledge and competencies, has become so important for our people's future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The place to do so informally is at our libraries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: No matter what stage we are in life, our public libraries are places for learning at your own comfort level and pace, where you can pick up a book or attend a talk, for your hobby or career.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Technology also enables our people to read and learn more conveniently, wherever they are, whenever they want to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To support this, Dr Teo Ho Pin has suggested we make e-books freely available and broadcast book reviews via smart phones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Take Samiksha, whom you saw in the video played earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: She is a busy student who downloads NLB's digital books and journals to read on the go.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Book summaries are also available via NLB's mobile app.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There is also Mr Foong Chow Weng, who uses the Pasir Ris Public Library often.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: He is 63 years old and has also made the switch to digital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: He began reading the newspapers online from digital devices at the library, after seeing a queue of people waiting to read the physical copies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: He enjoys reading the digital version, as he says he can "view all the newspapers at one place and zoom in to make the words bigger".

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Foong is, indeed, an example of a lifelong learner, adapting to new technologies to serve his learning needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: However, Sir, I also recognise that nothing can replace the feel of a book.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Some people, like myself, are more comfortable with them, so our libraries will continue to cater to all modes of reading and learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The key is to encourage everyone to use our libraries to read and learn.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Dr Teo Ho Pin has asked for a progress update on the National Reading Movement and what measures we have taken to inspire Singaporeans to read.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Darryl David has also asked what we are doing to promote a reading culture among all segments of society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The first National Reading Day on 30 July was a rallying call for the public to pledge to read more, read widely and read together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For example, DP Architects spread regular reading recommendations to their staff and participated in library programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: PropNex, KPMG and PhillipCapital Group respectively organised mass reading sessions, book exchanges and book review competitions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: NLB also launched a Curated Reads programme, which provides organisations a starter kit series of curated book excerpts, video clips and other smaller, bite-sized materials.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The topics ranged from values for life to skills for work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Companies, such as Singtel, have disseminated them to their staff.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Meanwhile, NLB has also increased the number of mother tongue programme offerings last year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To encourage the young to read in their mother tongues, it set up 11 mother tongue language reading clubs for children as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Besides the mother tongue language reading clubs, NLB has run the national KidsREAD programme for over 10 years now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It aims to promote the love of reading and cultivate good reading habits among children from low-income families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Last year, NLB refreshed the programme by introducing drama to KidsREAD.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The librarians and volunteers partnered expert storytellers and theatre companies to provide more varied styles of storytelling and dramatic, interactive performances of the storybooks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: They certainly enthralled beneficiaries like four-year-old Kai Yyi, who watched a dramatic retelling of a ninja story.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It was so exciting that the usually shy boy started raising his hand eagerly to answer questions and to interact with actors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Ms Sun Xueling has asked about how our libraries can inspire and inculcate the habit of lifelong learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I have said earlier that our libraries are places for learning, no matter what stage we are in life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: But libraries are also community places for our people to learn from one another, to come together and share their knowledge and experiences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For example, Matthew is an avid user of the PixelLab makers' space at Jurong Regional Library.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: He uses the 3D printers to create, modify and improve the parts for his self-made drones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: He has since founded a startup company making drones and happily shares his growing knowledge with other library users and the budding creative makers' community at Jurong library.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: People like Matthew who want to share their knowledge with others are an inspiration for NLB.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: That is why we want to evolve our libraries to foster more face-to-face connections, while still employing technology to meet the learning needs of Singaporeans and their digital lifestyles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We want our libraries to inspire people from all walks of life to come together as a community to learn together, learn from one another and embrace technology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To do so, we will redesign our library spaces and introduce programming that encourages collaborative learning and explore even more partnerships with the private and people sectors to promote reading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: They are designed to encourage collaboration and promote reading and learning as an attractive lifestyle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There are flexible seating and fixtures to enable discussion and creative expression, for example, at the Sengkang library's new Tween space.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There are also interactive digital displays where you can browse recommended digital books and download them via the NLB mobile app.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: At the much larger Bukit Panjang library, NLB will pilot a new immersive story-telling service for children aged four to 12.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Kids can soon experience the stories they hear with sound effects, lights and interactive, visual projections.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It will certainly be a new environment, which will complement the story-telling experience where librarians read aloud from picture books.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: NLB will also partner more communities and volunteers to encourage space co-ownership and community bonding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For example, seniors can soon gather and plan their own programmes in the new Bedok public library and, with training, even service their own corner of the new library in Tampines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There will also be a second makers' space and collaborative workspaces at the new Tampines Regional Library for budding entrepreneurs and creative makers to come to learn and experiment together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We had one in the West at Jurong, and now we will have another one in the East.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Ultimately, we want these new library spaces and programmes to spur our people towards a shared community journey of lifelong learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To gain insights on our current reading culture and habits, NLB recently completed an inaugural, nationwide study.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Nonetheless, our libraries are one of the top sources for books.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The study shows that we can do more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Dr Teo Ho Pin has also shared his views on how many Singaporeans are losing interest in reading books, especially among adults.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: While more must be done, NLB cannot do it alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: As shared by Ms Sun, we should work with the community to help different groups come together to learn together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Therefore, this year, for the National Reading Movement, NLB will seek more partnerships to encourage adults to read more and read widely.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Established business owners will share their knowledge and favourite reads.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will also continue to build a love of reading in our young.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: KidsREAD children can look forward to a new reading curriculum with more customised activities for different reading levels, and home activity packs that parents and guardians can use to read together with their children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This will not only help in building bonds but also sustain their interest in reading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Whether young or old, we must never stop learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: As the late Minister Mentor Lee once said, "One sign of an educated society is the number of books read by the people… one test of an educated man is his ability to continue reading and learning throughout his life".

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This was from Mr Lee's speech at the opening of the Queenstown library on 30 April 1970.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Lee was a living example of a lifelong learner who read widely throughout his life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Here, he is at the opening of the Nanyang University Library in 1966 and at a commemoration dinner in 2004, always reading, indeed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I hope that through our efforts in 2017, more Singaporeans will remember never to stop reading and learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Our NLB libraries will continue to play key roles in helping us do that.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The Committee on the Future Economy (CFE) has highlighted the need for Singapore to build strong digital capabilities so that we can participate fully in tomorrow's digital economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Like it or not, the digital economy is here to stay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Companies, citizens and even the Government will all have to make this transition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For businesses, the way markets are organised, the rise of the sharing and gig economy, and the global nature of competition on the Internet mean that companies must stay agile in order to adapt to the changing business environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: At the same time, companies have to accumulate and develop the expertise needed to manage and secure interconnected business systems and to extract insights from the massive amounts of data that they are gathering.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Individuals also need new skills to thrive in the digital economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Whether you are a professional harnessing technology to transform your business, a hobbyist learning coding in your free time, a content creator figuring out how to engage your audiences online, or a casual user navigating the rich universe of online media, we all need to know more about what going digital really means.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: My Ministry recognises this and has outlined our plans for IMDA to help Singaporeans gain new skills in ICM technologies through the TechSkills Accelerator programme to support media freelancers and to help businesses transform their operations and processes through digitalisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: At the same time, we have also highlighted our efforts to help companies protect and secure their valuable data and the steps we are taking to grow the cybersecurity profession in the process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Change is never easy, but we can minimise the dislocation we experience by understanding and preparing for it as early as we can by "doing, learning and adapting", as the Minister for Finance said last week.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We can best do this through partnership between the Government and businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Businesses must be proactive in maximising the potential of ICM technologies to deliver new services and products and even in exploring new emerging markets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Hence, I share Mr Ganesh Rajaram's views that our businesses should explore partnering competitors beyond our shores.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: But we also need highly connected cutting-edge companies prepared to grapple with the "innovator's dilemma'" head on in order to thrive in a digital economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The Government also needs to be highly connected and at the cutting edge of technology adoption in how it delivers public services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Citizens' expectations have increased and these make it incumbent on the Government to reach out to all Singaporeans and to build trust in new ways by leveraging technology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This means not only having the hardware and software in place but also the heartware.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Officers at our Citizen Connect Centres and our libraries can serve as ambassadors and guides to help the less tech-savvy users discover and maximise the benefits of transacting with the Government digitally on the go and at their own convenience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We cannot turn back the digital tide but we can ride it to a better destination.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: So, let us, therefore, come together − the Government, businesses, citizens, workers and civil society − to shape the digital Singapore we want.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Whether it is robotics, artificial intelligence or other new assistive technologies, which do we want to deploy and how?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Only when we come together can we realise the benefits of a truly digital economy, a truly digital society and a truly digital Government without leaving anyone behind.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: One, it is heartening to hear from the Minister the example of Mr Alvin Koh who is above 50 years old and who benefited from TeSA and is now a cybersecurity professional.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Many of those above 50 that I see, often find that careers and jobs are hard to come by.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: How can the Ministry help seniors in this age group find career pathways and, especially for those outside the sector, can we bring them in and how can we help them through?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The second question is about the transformation in sectors, such as the preschool sector.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I know this will help enhance experience of parents and children in this sector, but I just want to ask the Minister whether anchor operators and non-profit organisations will also be part of iSPRINT.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Because while these are not SMEs per se, they cater to a large base of lower-income children and families, and the impact can be quite significant.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The third supplementary question is for Minister of State Chee Hong Tat.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is heartening to know that for SPH, we have seen increased readership.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Part of my speech also covered the minority languages because we also want to make sure that there is sufficient coverage of that.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I know for The Straits Times and Lianhe Zaobao, there are existing programmes.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Are there also programmes for the Malay and Tamil newspapers as well to help enhance their reach and quality of journalism?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will assist them as much as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The reason why we want to do so is very simple.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There is, indeed, a shortage in the ICT sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The opportunities are there, like in cybersecurity and data analytics, but this is something which the individuals would have to make their choices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: What we will continue to do is to create more pathways by more partnerships with the companies and, through the partnerships, we hope that the companies can also see the value and the talent in some of the trainees so that they are willing to employ them after they have been trained.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We want to help as many as possible within the sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The preschool sector is a very large sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: IMDA is in conversation with the Early Childhood and Development Agency on how we can deploy some of these solutions across all members of that sector.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have programmes that are in place to support programmes, such as TV programmes and PSP programmes, on Suria for the Malay community, and on Vasantham for the Tamil community.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These additional resources that we have put in go into areas that include research, script development, content development, ultimately, to produce better quality local content that will resonate with the various groups of viewers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And what Suria and Vasantham do very well is also to follow up and bring the characters and shows from TV into real life.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, they do roadshows, they go into the heartlands, they engage their viewers using not just TV and radio, but bringing the stories, the characters face to face and interacting with the viewers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is something which I think can also extend to other channels.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In fact, these are good practices that I hope we can do likewise for the other channels on Mediacorp.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think the challenges are faced by all the newspapers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They need to continue to invest in producing good content and also the outreach, and moving in tandem with changing consumer preferences, which is why a lot of people are now viewing their news online using digital sources.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We also need to move online to be able to engage different groups of viewers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: One key learning point that the online teams have shared with me is that you cannot do online by taking traditional content and formats and going digital.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: You have to think online and design it online to meet the digital group of viewers and readers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The way you present your articles, the format which you use, the content which you use, all these need to be thought through and designed for what is the online audience.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will continue to work with our media companies, including SPH and Mediacorp, and across different languages and platforms.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Mr Chairman, following up on the topic of languages, I wonder if the Minister of State has any update on the work of the National Translation Committee.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I think Minister of State Chee Hong Tat discussed that in the last COS.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Mr Vikram Nair for his question on translation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I did not have time to cover that in my speech during the earlier session.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: To communicate effectively, we need to develop capabilities in effective translation.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: My belief is that we have got to start young to cultivate their interests, raise the awareness and also be able to develop the language skills.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have got strong collaboration with Berita Harian and also with MOE.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We organised the workshop for the Malay language translation, competition and we got young people to participate, raise awareness and interest.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: From what I discussed with the young people, they want to see more of such activities and make it fun for them, to show translation not as a very technical subject, but something that is fun and relevant and they can see how it can be applied in their daily lives.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I must thank our resource panel, chaired by Mr A Palaniappan.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They helped us develop a set of recommendations to further enhance the way we do Tamil translation in the Government.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I think this is the approach that we will continue to take.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Reaching out to the various communities, working with partners, raising standards, raising awareness.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I believe that translation is something which will give us not just a better way of appreciating the different languages that we have, better way of understanding the different cultures that we have, but it is also an effective way to communicate with different groups of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to thank Minister of State Chee for some add-on information that he gave with respect to my cut.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just two quick questions for Minister of State Chee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Can I seek confirmation from the Minister of State that the delayed broadcasts for Parliamentary Questions and Answers and Members' speeches will actually be reproduced in full and not edited when uploaded after Parliament has finished, so that there is no cut and nothing has been edited?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I just want confirmation from the Minister of State on that point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I say this because I do believe that public discussion on policy matters actually would be improved and would be more reasoned as a result of "live" Parliamentary broadcasts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Mr Pritam Singh for his questions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For the speeches, I think Mr Pritam Singh would probably know this, many of us would go to the site and use those videos for social media.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As I said earlier in my speech, it is out there for up to six months of archival period.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On the second question, I thank Mr Singh for acknowledging that there are pros and cons to "live" broadcasts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We do recognise the upside as well; it is not that this is a straightforward thing.
